title: A bishop is worth the lines it attacks, not the square it stands on. A protected outpost is a knight's measure.

positions.why: The bishop looks well placed on b5: deep in Black's half and held by the a4 pawn. But follow its diagonals: they end on empty squares. One square away, on c4, its diagonal runs through e6 to the king on g8, and the rook is pinned: 1. Bc4 Kf7 2. Re1, and it is lost. A protected outpost is how you judge a knight's square. A bishop's is judged by what stands on its lines.

title: Don't castle, or step the king, into pressure: go where your defenders outnumber their attackers.

positions.why: Both ways of castling are legal; look at what each side of the board holds. On the kingside Black's queen and d6 bishop are lined up on h2, the g4 bishop is ready to take the knight that guards it, and a knight is a jump away: 1. O-O Bxf3 2. gxf3 Ne5, and your king has no cover left. On the queenside nothing of Black's points at your king, and the same capture only hands you the open g-file: 1. O-O-O Bxf3 2. gxf3, and the h-pawn is not hanging: 2... Bxh2 3. f4 shuts the queen out and wins the bishop. Castle where your defenders outnumber their attackers.

title: Before judging an attack on a king, count the attackers and the defenders that can reach that side, and how many moves each needs.

positions.source: composed (the classic bishop sacrifice on h7)
positions.why: A sacrifice on h7 is a count, not a guess. Attackers that reach the king within two moves: the bishop (now), the knight (Ng5+), the queen (Qh5), with the c1 bishop behind g5. Defenders that can get there: no knight to f6, because your e5 pawn takes it; the c8 bishop is shut in by e6; the queen can only give itself up on g5. Three against none, so 1. Bxh7+ Kxh7 2. Ng5+ Kg8 3. Qh5, and Black must play 3... Qxg5 to stop mate. 2... Kg6 3. Qd3+ is no better.

title: Always look for the mating lines, yours and theirs: a mate threat forces the reply, so it decides the other moves.

positions.why: Look for the mate first. Queen and bishop together on the diagonal to h7 would mate there, since Black's own bishop takes f8 from his king. 1. Qe4 threatens exactly that. Because it is mate, Black has to spend his move on it (1... g6 or 1... f5), and the queen on e4 attacks something else as well: the rook on a8, which the b8 knight cuts off from its defenders. 2. Qxa8. A mate threat is a free move: ask what else the threatening piece attacks.

title: To promote a passed pawn, secure the promotion square first.

positions.why: The pawn needs d6, d7 and d8, and Black's king is sitting on d8. Push now and it gets no further: 1. d6 Ke8 2. d7+ Kd8 3. Kd6 is stalemate. The king has to take the squares first. 1. Kd6 puts it in front of the pawn: after 1... Ke8 2. Kc7 (or 1... Kc8 2. Ke7) it guards d7 and d8, and the pawn walks home behind it. Every other move only draws.

title: In the endgame, ask whether you can safely activate your king.

positions.why: Black is a pawn up, and the pawn is on e4, a long way from its king. Nothing on the board can hurt your king, so ask only how fast it gets there: f2, e3, and it takes on e4 on move three. Black's king needs three moves to protect the pawn and has only two: 1. Kf2 Kf7 2. Ke3 Kf6 3. Kxe4, with level pawns. A move later is too late: 1. a4 Kf7 2. Kf2 Ke6 3. Ke3 Ke5, and Black keeps the pawn and wins.

title: In the endgame, a rook on the second-to-last rank often shuts the enemy king in completely.

positions.why: Black is one move from ...Kd7, when his king guards c7 and comes to the centre. The rook gets in first: 1. Rc7. On the seventh rank it attacks b7 and g7 at once, and it shuts the king in on the back rank: d7 and e7 are both taken from it. A pawn falls (1... Kf8 2. Rxb7) and the king is still a spectator. After a slow move the chance is gone: 1. Kf2 Kd7, and the game is level.

title: In the endgame, take squares away from the enemy king so that it cannot join in.

positions.why: Rook and pawn against rook. If Black's king gets in front of the c-pawn the game is drawn, and it needs only to cross the e-file. 1. Re1 takes that file away: the king is held two files from the pawn, and White's king and pawn advance with only the rook to trouble them. It is the only winning move; after anything else the king comes across and the position is a draw. The enemy king is a defender: before pushing, ask which file or rank your rook can deny it.

title: Two knights diagonal to each other do not guard each other yet: one move by either and they do.

positions.why: You are a knight up, but the d4 knight is attacked twice, by rook and bishop, and guarded once. It cannot move: the rook behind it would fall with check. Counter-attack does not help: 1. Nc4, hitting the bishop, gives the piece back after 1... Rxd4 2. Rxd4 Bxd4. The knights stand diagonal to each other, on d4 and e5: neither guards the other yet, and one move by the free one makes them. 1. Nef3 covers d4 a second time, and the extra piece stays.

title: Check for opponent pieces that have no squares to move to, and attack those.

positions.source: opening theory (the Noah's Ark trap in the Ruy Lopez)
positions.why: Look at White's bishop on b3. Its retreats are gone: a4 and c4 are covered by your b5 pawn, and a2 and c2 hold its own pawns. Only d5 is left, and a pawn on c4 would attack it. So attack it, and gain the move to do so: 8... c5 hits the queen first, and ...c4 comes next. After 9. Qd5 Be6 10. Qc6+ Bd7 11. Qd5 c4 the bishop is lost. A piece with no squares needs to be attacked only once.

title: Two unprotected pieces on one line are a target: an attack on the front one wins the one behind.

positions.why: Black's two bishops stand on one file, b6 in front of b7, and nothing protects either. Neither can ever guard the other, and no black piece can reach them in one move. That is a target: 1. Rb1 attacks the front one, and when it moves the rook takes the one behind (1... Bd4 2. Rxb7, or 1... Bc6 2. Rxb6). Look for the same picture in your own position before an attacking move: a piece and a pawn on one file, both loose, are won the same way by a queen.

title: Before moving a piece, ask what it is guarding where it stands.

positions.why: Black has just taken a knight on d4, and two pieces can take back. Ask each what it is doing where it stands. The f3 knight is the only guard of h2, with Black's queen and bishop lined up on it: 1. Nxd4 Qxh2 is mate. The queen guards nothing that matters: 1. Qxd4 Qxd4 2. Nxd4, and the game is level. Leaving the knight where it is does not help either: 1. g3 Ne2+.

title: Before you attack or grab something, list the opponent's checks and captures in reply.

positions.why: The queen on b2 can be attacked at once by 6. Bc3. Before attacking, list Black's replies: 6... Bb4 pins that bishop to your king. Then 7. Bxb4 Qxa1 loses the rook, and 7. Qd2 Bxc3 8. Qxc3 Qc1 is mate. The developing move 6. Nc3 leaves the pin and the checks nothing to work on, and now it is the queen that must run: 6... Bb4 7. Rb1 Qa3 8. Rb3. Your own threat is half the picture; their checks and captures in reply are the other half.

title: Before a check or a sacrifice, ask what your next move is after the reply. If there is none, don't play it.

positions.why: Your bishop on f4 is attacked by the knight, and 16. Qa4+ is a check. Ask what you play after the reply: 16... b5 blocks it with an attack on your queen, the queen has to move again, and the bishop is still hanging: 17. Qd1 Nxf4. There was no second move behind the check. 16. Qf3 does three jobs without one: it guards the bishop, it aims at f7, and it pins the d5 knight to the unprotected queen on b7 (16... Nxf4 17. Qxb7).

title: Before a trade, picture the recapture: which piece lands where, and what it does from there.

positions.why: You are in check from the bishop, and trading it off looks natural. Picture the recapture first: 23... Bxd5 24. Qxd5+ brings the queen to d5 with another check, and from there it attacks the knight on d7 as well, which falls next move (24... Kh8 25. Qxd7). Step aside and there is nothing of the kind: 23... Kh8 (on h7 the king runs into Qd3+), and after 24. Rxc8 Qxc8 25. Bxb7 Qxb7 26. Rxf8+ Nxf8 you are still a piece up.

title: When something of yours is attacked, look first for the answer that also attacks.

positions.source: a game of yours, from the opponent's side (456267ee, move 8)
positions.why: You are in check, and the knight on a5 is attacked as well. 8... Nc6 answers both and does nothing else: 9. Qxb7. Look for the reply that makes a threat of its own: 8... c6 blocks the check by attacking the queen, and it opens the diagonal from d8 to a5, so your queen now guards the knight. White has to move the queen, and nothing is lost. (Allie had this position against you and played 8... Qd7, losing the knight to 9. Qxa5.)

title: A pawn move or a pawn capture opens lines. Before one near a king, ask which, and who is already on them.

positions.why: Black's knight has taken a piece on g3, and two pawns can take it back. Ask which line each capture opens, and who is already on it. 1. hxg3 opens the h-file, where Black's queen and rook are doubled: 1... Qh1 is mate. 1. fxg3 opens two lines for you instead: the f-file for your rook, and the second rank, along which your queen now guards h2. You stay a piece up: 1... Qb6+ 2. Qf2.

title: Before a piece lands, ask what can hit it there: knights and pawns first.

positions.why: Black has just taken a bishop on d3, and the queen can take back. Before it lands there, ask what can hit it on d3: the pawn on e5. 1. Qxd3 e4 attacks the queen and the f3 knight together, and a piece goes. Take with the pawn instead: 1. cxd3. Now ...e4 forks nothing, and the pawn on d3 can simply take it.

title: When two moves both belong to the idea, play first the one that will not be there next move.

positions.why: Two black pieces can be taken: the rook on a2 by your knight, the knight on g4 by your pawn. Take first the one that can run away. The rook is shut in: a1 is covered by your rook, and the pawns on a3 and b2 are both guarded, so it will still be there next move. The knight will not. 1. hxg4 Rxb2 2. Rxb2 wins both; 1. Nxa2 Ne5 wins only the rook. The bigger piece is not always the one to take first.

title: In the opening, when a pawn can take the centre with tempo (e4, d5), play it before the quiet developing move.

positions.source: opening theory (the fork trick against 4. Nc3 in the Italian)
positions.why: You have given a knight for the e4 pawn, and on purpose: White's bishop on c4 and knight on e4 stand side by side. A centre pawn takes its square with tempo and wins the piece back: 5... d5 attacks both. After 6. Bd3 dxe4 7. Bxe4 Bd6 material is level, and you have a pawn in the centre and free development. When a pawn can take the centre by hitting a piece, it comes before any developing move.

title: When a piece takes a pawn deep in your camp, don't end the line there: trace its way back out, and ask what of yours can step onto it.

positions.source: composed: the king-into-pressure position after 1. O-O-O Bxf3 2. gxf3 Bxh2, the line the student wanted to prevent with 1. Be2 (2026-11-24)
positions.why: Black's bishop has just taken on h2: the capture that looked worth a whole move to prevent. Don't end the line on his capture; trace the bishop's way back. It has one diagonal, h2 to c7, and that same diagonal is how the queen guards it. The pawn you know for this is g3, and the g-pawn is gone. But the square does not matter, the diagonal does: 1. f4 steps onto it one square further along. Now the rook attacks the bishop, nothing guards it, and every way out loses it: 1... Bxf4 2. Bxf4, 1... Bg3 2. fxg3, 1... Bg1 2. Rdxg1. A piece for two pawns, with the g- and h-files open for your rooks. Taking back at once misses it: 1. Rxh2 Qxh2 gives a rook for the bishop. So the capture was never a threat, and no move had to be spent on stopping it.
